input.summary: The application now reads as one finished draft of the split pipe clamp: 17 claims in three statutory classes (clamp, installed clamp assembly, method), a description carrying only what the inventor disclosed, four figure briefs whose numeral declarations and sheet lists agree, and a numeral table of 28 numerals every one of which is used in the description and appears on a sheet. This turn I brought the Summary, Background, abstract, numeral table and claim ladder into line with the description, which had already been stripped of the candidate-introduced structure the reviewer identified. Specifically: the Summary's assertions that the grip is taken around the whole arc rather than across the split line, that the latch does not hold the working load, that the operator can station the clamp along the pipe in the first latch position, that no separate coupling step is asked of the operator, and that a load on the mounting boss cannot disturb the cam drive are all gone, because none of them appears in the inventor's material. The Background no longer asserts what existing clamps do or how they fail in service; it states the mechanical problem analytically ("Where the grip is obtained by drawing the two frame halves toward one another, the closing force enters the frame at the split line"), which is the form a later argument can be built on without resting on facts nobody supplied. Numeral 68 (the over-center link) is deleted from the table; the word "over-center" survives only as the disclosed latch position. Two review findings I did not act on, with reasons: the review's three failing mechanical checks (numerals absent from every drawing, brief declarations not matching sheet lists, no drawing sheet for FIG. 1 to FIG. 4) were artifacts of the figure files being named fig-01.md through fig-04.md at review time; they are now FIG-1.md through FIG-4.md, each brief declares exactly the numerals in its own machine-readable list, and the union of the four lists is the whole numeral table, so there is nothing left to repair in the briefs themselves. The reviewer's suggestion that the description be widened is likewise moot: I narrowed the claims to the description rather than the other way round. One thing you should know: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references at all, so this draft contains no citation and no reference was written around. The art available to this draft may be incomplete, and claim 1 has been positioned only against the disclosure itself, not against any searched art.
reasoning: Claim 1 now carries the whole of the inventor's stated essential relationship: the cam ring split into a segment per frame half, coupled by complementary drive faces at both the hinge end and the latch end when the halves close; a latch-carried wedge bearing on a ring drive face to rotate that coupled ring through a limited stroke; followers in oblique slots turning the single rotation into common inward travel; and the force-limiting spring stack in the drive path between latch handle and wedge. The reviewer flagged that the earlier claim 1 omitted the spring stack and therefore covered a clamp the disclosure never presents. I agreed and moved it up. It costs little scope, because a clamp with this cam-ring coupling but no force limiter is not what the inventor described, and it gives the claim a second independent point of argument if the coupling feature is ever met.

The feature doing the real work in claim 1 is that the drive ring is itself divided and is made whole by the act of closing the frame, at two separate interfaces, so the drive train exists only in the closed condition. That is what carries the claim away from the ordinary split clamp, whose tightening motion crosses the split line, and away from a one-piece scroll or cam collar, which cannot be opened around an installed pipe at all. I could not name a reference that this clears, because prior_art/INDEX.md lists none.

I kept three jaw carriages in claim 1 rather than 'a plurality'. The disclosure fixes the count at three and gives no other number; the earlier draft supported 'plurality' with an invented sentence about clamps having more than three, which the reviewer correctly struck. Once that sentence is gone, a plurality claim has no written-description support behind it, so I took the narrower count that is fully supported over broader words that are not.

Deliberately left out of claim 1: any bounding structure for the limited stroke, any form for the follower, any pad pivot axis, any apportionment of the radial guides between the halves, and any inclination relationship for the ring drive face. Each was in the earlier claim set as a dependent, and each rested on structure the candidate had supplied rather than the inventor. Omitting an unsupported optional limitation is cheaper than defending it.

New dependent claim 3 recites that the clamping load is set by the spring stack rather than by where the latch comes to rest, and new dependent claim 10 recites that the pivoting pad bears on a pipe without requiring a tool specific pipe diameter. Both are word-for-word supported in the description, and both are separately arguable: claim 3 is about what determines the load, claim 10 about what determines the size range. They give the ladder two genuinely different footholds below claim 1 rather than aesthetic narrowing.

The dependent ladder is ordered as fallbacks first, then different embodiments: spring-stack behaviour (2, 3), the indicator (4), the two latch positions (5), the slot geometry that makes travel equal at every carriage (6), the segments separating with their own halves on opening (7), the mounting boss standing clear of the drive (8), the spring return (9), the diameter tolerance (10).

The assembly claim (11) and the method claim (14) are drafted to be infringed by different parties: the assembly claim reaches an installed clamp on a pipe, the method claim reaches the installer. Both recite the spring stack, so neither is broader than claim 1 in the one respect the inventor calls essential. I added the sentence to the description stating that the clamp and the pipe form an installed clamp assembly when closed and clamped, so the assembly claims use the description's own term.

Claim 12 was reworded from 'stands at a position relative to a fixed edge' to the description's own formulation, an indicator pin visible on the latch that moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the stack enters a predetermined compression range. Same element, one name, in both documents.

The Background had to be rewritten rather than trimmed, because its force came from asserted facts about how existing clamps behave in service. I kept the technical problems the invention answers, which the disclosure itself implies (a divided frame has to be tightened; jaws advanced one at a time have to be balanced by the operator; a quick acting latch closes to the same position whether or not the jaws are loaded), but stated them as consequences of the arrangement rather than as reports of what the art does.

Figure work: no figure was changed this turn. The four briefs already show the pads, not the carriages, meeting the pipe in FIG. 1, a plain schematic drive face on the ring in FIG. 3 in place of the invented lug with its inclined flank, and in FIG. 4 a handle joined to the housing and reaching onto the spring stack with no link and no opening in the housing top wall. Each sheet lists at most eight numerals and each brief is under 2800 characters.

The draft therefore contains no [REF:...] citation, and the Background makes no statement about any identified document. Because no art was supplied, I could not point to a reference that a given limitation clears. Instead I made claim 1 turn on the relationship the inventor calls essential and which is the least likely to be met by a general-purpose pipe clamp: the drive ring is divided into one segment per frame half, each segment stays with its own half when the clamp is opened, and closing the halves brings complementary drive faces into engagement at both the hinge end and the latch end so that the two segments rotate as one ring. The drive train exists only when the frame is closed, and the wedge on the latch then rotates that reassembled ring through a limited stroke while oblique slots convert the single rotation into common inward travel at every carriage, with a force-limiting spring stack in the drive path taking up the latch travel left over after the pads touch down. A conventional split clamp tightens by pulling its halves together across the split line, and a one-piece scroll or cam chuck cannot be opened around an installed pipe; the recited combination is neither. The specification states the technical problems these features answer, the divided frame that must nonetheless carry a continuous drive and the variable residual latch travel that would otherwise be forced into one jaw, so the argument material is in the document before it is needed. The art given to this draft may be incomplete, and this positioning should be re-tested once a search has been run.

This turn I brought the Summary, Background, abstract, numeral table and claim ladder into line with the description, which had already been stripped of the candidate-introduced structure the reviewer identified. Specifically: the Summary's assertions that the grip is taken around the whole arc rather than across the split line, that the latch does not hold the working load, that the operator can station the clamp along the pipe in the first latch position, that no separate coupling step is asked of the operator, and that a load on the mounting boss cannot disturb the cam drive are all gone, because none of them appears in the inventor's material. The Background no longer asserts what existing clamps do or how they fail in service; it states the mechanical problem analytically ("Where the grip is obtained by drawing the two frame halves toward one another, the closing force enters the frame at the split line"), which is the form a later argument can be built on without resting on facts nobody supplied. Numeral 68 (the over-center link) is deleted from the table; the word "over-center" survives only as the disclosed latch position. Two review findings I did not act on, with reasons: the review's three failing mechanical checks (numerals absent from every drawing, brief declarations not matching sheet lists, no drawing sheet for FIG. 1 to FIG. 4) were artifacts of the figure files being named fig-01.md through fig-04.md at review time; they are now FIG-1.md through FIG-4.md, each brief declares exactly the numerals in its own machine-readable list, and the union of the four lists is the whole numeral table, so there is nothing left to repair in the briefs themselves. The reviewer's suggestion that the description be widened is likewise moot: I narrowed the claims to the description rather than the other way round. One thing you should know: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references at all, so this draft contains no citation and no reference was written around. The art available to this draft may be incomplete, and claim 1 has been positioned only against the disclosure itself, not against any searched art.
reasoning: Claim 1 now carries the whole of the inventor's stated essential relationship: the cam ring split into a segment per frame half, coupled by complementary drive faces at both the hinge end and the latch end when the halves close; a latch-carried wedge bearing on a ring drive face to rotate that coupled ring through a limited stroke; followers in oblique slots turning the single rotation into common inward travel; and the force-limiting spring stack in the drive path between latch handle and wedge. The reviewer flagged that the earlier claim 1 omitted the spring stack and therefore covered a clamp the disclosure never presents. I agreed and moved it up. It costs little scope, because a clamp with this cam-ring coupling but no force limiter is not what the inventor described, and it gives the claim a second independent point of argument if the coupling feature is ever met.

The feature doing the real work in claim 1 is that the drive ring is itself divided and is made whole by the act of closing the frame, at two separate interfaces, so the drive train exists only in the closed condition. That is what carries the claim away from the ordinary split clamp, whose tightening motion crosses the split line, and away from a one-piece scroll or cam collar, which cannot be opened around an installed pipe at all. I could not name a reference that this clears, because prior_art/INDEX.md lists none.

I kept three jaw carriages in claim 1 rather than 'a plurality'. The disclosure fixes the count at three and gives no other number; the earlier draft supported 'plurality' with an invented sentence about clamps having more than three, which the reviewer correctly struck. Once that sentence is gone, a plurality claim has no written-description support behind it, so I took the narrower count that is fully supported over broader words that are not.

Deliberately left out of claim 1: any bounding structure for the limited stroke, any form for the follower, any pad pivot axis, any apportionment of the radial guides between the halves, and any inclination relationship for the ring drive face. Each was in the earlier claim set as a dependent, and each rested on structure the candidate had supplied rather than the inventor. Omitting an unsupported optional limitation is cheaper than defending it.

New dependent claim 3 recites that the clamping load is set by the spring stack rather than by where the latch comes to rest, and new dependent claim 10 recites that the pivoting pad bears on a pipe without requiring a tool specific pipe diameter. Both are word-for-word supported in the description, and both are separately arguable: claim 3 is about what determines the load, claim 10 about what determines the size range. They give the ladder two genuinely different footholds below claim 1 rather than aesthetic narrowing.

The dependent ladder is ordered as fallbacks first, then different embodiments: spring-stack behaviour (2, 3), the indicator (4), the two latch positions (5), the slot geometry that makes travel equal at every carriage (6), the segments separating with their own halves on opening (7), the mounting boss standing clear of the drive (8), the spring return (9), the diameter tolerance (10).

The assembly claim (11) and the method claim (14) are drafted to be infringed by different parties: the assembly claim reaches an installed clamp on a pipe, the method claim reaches the installer. Both recite the spring stack, so neither is broader than claim 1 in the one respect the inventor calls essential. I added the sentence to the description stating that the clamp and the pipe form an installed clamp assembly when closed and clamped, so the assembly claims use the description's own term.

Claim 12 was reworded from 'stands at a position relative to a fixed edge' to the description's own formulation, an indicator pin visible on the latch that moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the stack enters a predetermined compression range. Same element, one name, in both documents.

The Background had to be rewritten rather than trimmed, because its force came from asserted facts about how existing clamps behave in service. I kept the technical problems the invention answers, which the disclosure itself implies (a divided frame has to be tightened; jaws advanced one at a time have to be balanced by the operator; a quick acting latch closes to the same position whether or not the jaws are loaded), but stated them as consequences of the arrangement rather than as reports of what the art does.

Figure work: no figure was changed this turn. The four briefs already show the pads, not the carriages, meeting the pipe in FIG. 1, a plain schematic drive face on the ring in FIG. 3 in place of the invented lug with its inclined flank, and in FIG. 4 a handle joined to the housing and reaching onto the spring stack with no link and no opening in the housing top wall. In the following description, like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views. The described arrangement is one form of the invention and is not a limitation on the scope of the claims. Terms of orientation such as inward, outward, radial and circumferential are used with reference to a central axis of the closed frame, which in use is substantially coincident with the axis of the pipe being gripped.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a split pipe clamp 10 comprises a first frame half 12 and a second frame half 14. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are each substantially semicircular, and together they define a frame that surrounds a pipe 20 when closed. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are joined at a hinge end of the frame by a hinge 16 and are releasably joined at a latch end of the frame, opposite the hinge end, by a releasable latch 18. Swinging the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16 opens the frame laterally, so that the split pipe clamp 10 can be applied to a pipe 20 that is already installed and that cannot be entered from a free end. The split pipe clamp 10 and the pipe 20 together form an installed clamp assembly when the split pipe clamp 10 is closed and clamped on the pipe 20.

Three jaw carriages 22 are distributed circumferentially about the closed frame, as shown in FIG. 1.

The frame carries a mounting boss 66. The mounting boss 66 supports a sensor, a tool or a conduit on the split pipe clamp 10. The mounting boss 66 does not participate in advancing or synchronizing the jaw carriages 22.

Jaw carriages and jaw pads

Referring to FIG. 2, each jaw carriage 22 is slidable in a respective radial guide 24 of the frame. The radial guide 24 constrains the jaw carriage 22 to travel along a radial path toward and away from the central axis of the closed frame.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a jaw pad 26 that is mounted on the jaw carriage 22 for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface toward the central axis of the closed frame. Because the jaw pad 26 pivots relative to the jaw carriage 22, the jaw pad 26 bears on the pipe 20 without requiring a tool specific pipe diameter.

A carriage spring 42 biases each jaw carriage 22 outward, away from the central axis of the closed frame. When the releasable latch 18 is released, the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22 outward and lift the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened.

The segmented cam ring

A cam ring 30 is retained in an annular guide 36 of the frame, as shown in FIG. 2. The annular guide 36 is an annular channel of the frame, concentric with the central axis of the closed frame, that retains the cam ring 30 while allowing the cam ring 30 to rotate through a limited stroke about that axis.

The mounting boss 66 stands on the frame outside the annular guide 36, clear of the cam ring 30 and of the jaw carriages 22.

The cam ring 30 is segmented. Referring to FIG. 3, the cam ring 30 comprises a first cam-ring segment 32 and a second cam-ring segment 34. The first cam-ring segment 32 is carried by the first frame half 12 and the second cam-ring segment 34 is carried by the second frame half 14, each segment being retained by the frame half that carries it. Each segment accordingly stays with its own frame half when the frame is opened, and the frame halves can be swung apart without dismantling the drive.

The first cam-ring segment 32 has a hinge-end drive face 44 and a latch-end drive face 48. The second cam-ring segment 34 has a hinge-end drive face 46 and a latch-end drive face 50. The hinge-end drive face 44 and the hinge-end drive face 46 are complementary to one another, and the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 are complementary to one another. Closing the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 at the hinge end and brings the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50 at the latch end, and thereby couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 so that they rotate together as one cam ring 30 about the central axis of the closed frame.

In the closed frame each pair of complementary drive faces transmits circumferential drive from one cam-ring segment to the other, and the complementary drive faces separate when the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are swung apart about the hinge 16.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a follower 40 that is received in a respective oblique slot 38 of the cam ring 30, as shown in FIG. 2. Each oblique slot 38 is inclined to the circumferential direction of the cam ring 30, so that rotation of the cam ring 30 through the limited stroke displaces the follower 40, and with it the jaw carriage 22, along the radial guide 24. The oblique slots 38 are identical in inclination and are distributed circumferentially to match the jaw carriages 22, so that rotation of the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke produces the same inward travel at every jaw carriage 22. The inward travel of the three jaw carriages 22 is thereby synchronized.

The latch drive

The releasable latch 18 carries a wedge 52, as shown in FIG. 4. Moving the releasable latch 18 drives the wedge 52 against a ring drive face 54 of the cam ring 30, shown in FIG. 3, and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke.

The releasable latch 18 has a first position and a second position. In the first position the releasable latch 18 holds the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 around the pipe 20 without clamping the pipe 20. The second position is an over-center position, in which the releasable latch 18 has driven the wedge 52 and the cam ring 30 and clamps the pipe 20.

Referring again to FIG. 4, the releasable latch 18 comprises a latch handle 56, a latch housing 58 and a force-limiting spring stack 62. The force-limiting spring stack 62 lies in a drive path between the latch handle 56 and the wedge 52.

Once all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, further movement of the latch handle 56 toward the over-center position compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than forcing one jaw pad 26 farther than the others. The latch travel that remains after contact is therefore taken up by the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the clamping load is set by the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than by the position at which the releasable latch 18 comes to rest.

An indicator pin 64 is visible on the releasable latch 18 and moves relative to a fixed edge 60 of the latch housing 58 when the force-limiting spring stack 62 enters a predetermined compression range. The position of the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60 is a mechanical report that the split pipe clamp 10 is loaded within that range. The indicator pin 64 reports clamp loading and does not measure the diameter of the pipe 20.

Installation and removal

To install the split pipe clamp 10, an operator opens the releasable latch 18 and swings the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 20 and closes them, which brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 and the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50, and so couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 into a single cam ring 30. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the first position, in which the frame halves are held around the pipe 20 without clamping. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the over-center position. The wedge 52 bears on the ring drive face 54 and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke, the oblique slots 38 advance all of the jaw carriages 22 inward together, and the jaw pads 26 pivot and seat on the pipe 20. Latch travel remaining after the jaw pads 26 seat compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the operator observes the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60.

To remove the split pipe clamp 10, the operator releases the releasable latch 18. The force-limiting spring stack 62 unloads and the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22, lifting the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are then swung apart about the hinge 16, and the hinge-end drive face 44, the hinge-end drive face 46, the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 separate so that the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 travel with their own frame halves. The split pipe clamp 10 is reusable.

The essential relationship of the arrangement described here is that closure of the frame halves couples the cam-ring segments, that travel of the releasable latch 18 drives the coupled cam ring 30, that the oblique slots 38 synchronize the radial travel of the jaw carriages 22, and that the force-limiting spring stack 62 accommodates the remaining latch travel. The features described above may be combined in ways other than those expressly set out, and modifications within the understanding of a person skilled in the art fall within the scope of the claims that follow.

disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.

shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded

outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than

1	# Previous review - verdict: fail
2	
3	Ledger result: the great majority of the application text traces cleanly to the single USER disclosure passage (which is reproduced verbatim in conversation.md). Claims 1-5, 7, 9-17, the Field, Summary, Abstract, Detailed Description narrative, the numeral table, and FIG. 1 / FIG. 2 in substance all map to affirmative inventor sentences: split semicircular halves with hinge at one end and releasable latch at the other; three radial jaw carriages in radial guides with pivoting concave pads; a segmented cam ring in an annular guide with one segment per frame half; complementary hinge-end and latch-end drive faces coupled by frame closure; followers in oblique slots; a wedge driven against a ring drive face through a limited stroke; carriage springs biasing outward; two latch positions with an over-center second position; a force-limiting spring stack between handle and wedge; a visible indicator pin moving relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing over a predetermined compression range; the install/remove sequences; and the non-participating mounting boss outside the annular guide. Cross-reference and government-support sections match brief.md ("No priority claim. No federally sponsored research"). Background prior-art characterizations are not traced here by design. No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions, or unresolved alternatives remain in the application text, and no "by way of example"/"any closed outline" style justification of a renderer's choice appears in the description or Brief Description. Numerals are one-to-one with parts, section-line designations are not used (FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 are stated as an omitted-near-side view and a cutaway, with matching language in 07-drawings.md and the briefs), and the four figure titles agree between 07-drawings.md and the briefs.
4	
5	Nine problems were verified. Two are untraced limitations that reach the claims: (1) "the oblique slots are identical in inclination" (claim 6 and description ¶ on FIG. 2) adds slot-geometry structure the inventor never stated - the source says only that the slots "translate that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three jaw carriages"; and (2) "the mounting boss being clear of the cam ring and of the jaw carriages" (claim 8 and description) converts the inventor's functional statement ("The mounting boss does not participate in jaw synchronization") into an untraced spatial relationship, since a boss outside the annular guide could still overlie a radial jaw carriage.
6	
7	The remaining problems are in the figure briefs, all in areas the preflight treats as substantive even under a schematic label. FIG-3 verbalizes the radial and circumferential position of the ring drive face 54 ("On the outer side of the band, between the right junction and the slot at the lower right ... drawn on the outer boundary of the band"); the disclosure says only that the latch "drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring." That placement is doubly problematic because a plain face lying along the outer boundary, struck radially inward by the wedge, would not deliver the circumferential drive the description requires. FIG-4 invents a drive-path sub-mechanism: top and bottom plates closing the spring-stack column, with the handle's inner arm "resting on" the upper plate and the wedge below the lower plate; the inventor discloses only that the stack "lies between the latch handle and the wedge." FIG-4 also mounts the indicator pin on that invented upper plate and assigns the "fixed edge" to the housing top wall, neither of which is in the source, and it then encloses the pin entirely inside the housing - which contradicts the description's "An indicator pin 64 is visible on the releasable latch 18" and "the operator observes the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60," since in the brief the pin is visible only because the near wall is cut away. FIG-4 further routes the wedge "downward out of the housing through the arcuate band, its inclined face visible below the band," asserting an untraced penetration of an unidentified, unnumbered frame band and a specific taper direction. Two minor items: FIG-2 anchors each carriage spring "in the outer stretch of each slideway ... at its outer end to the frame at the outer circle," choosing a tension-outboard arrangement the source does not specify beyond "A spring biases each carriage outward"; and FIG-4 places numeral 18 (latch as a whole) on the right side wall of the same housing that numeral 58 (latch housing) marks on the left, which invites a two-meanings reading of one structure.
8	
9	Items considered and cleared: roughly equal angular spacing of the three carriages and three slots (fairly read from "Three radial jaw carriages are distributed around the closed frame" plus synchronized travel); the pads' concave inner edges and pin-circle pivots; the "installed clamp assembly" statutory framing of claim 11 (the source has the clamp bearing on a pipe); claim 3's "clamping load ... set by the force-limiting spring stack" (implicit in a force-limiting stack that takes up remaining travel); FIG-3's matching end faces at the two junctions, whose shape is expressly left schematic; and FIG-1's schematic hinge, latch body, and boss pad. Every finding below carries a filing-clean fix; applying them leaves the claims and description shape-neutral and confines all depiction conventions to the figure briefs.

In the following description, like reference numerals designate like parts throughout the several views. The described arrangement is one form of the invention and is not a limitation on the scope of the claims. Terms of orientation such as inward, outward, radial and circumferential are used with reference to a central axis of the closed frame, which in use is substantially coincident with the axis of the pipe being gripped.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a split pipe clamp 10 comprises a first frame half 12 and a second frame half 14. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are each substantially semicircular, and together they define a frame that surrounds a pipe 20 when closed. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are joined at a hinge end of the frame by a hinge 16 and are releasably joined at a latch end of the frame, opposite the hinge end, by a releasable latch 18. Swinging the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16 opens the frame laterally, so that the split pipe clamp 10 can be applied to a pipe 20 that is already installed and that cannot be entered from a free end. The split pipe clamp 10 and the pipe 20 together form an installed clamp assembly when the split pipe clamp 10 is closed and clamped on the pipe 20.

Three jaw carriages 22 are distributed circumferentially about the closed frame, as shown in FIG. 1.

The frame carries a mounting boss 66. The mounting boss 66 supports a sensor, a tool or a conduit on the split pipe clamp 10. The mounting boss 66 does not participate in advancing or synchronizing the jaw carriages 22.

Jaw carriages and jaw pads

Referring to FIG. 2, each jaw carriage 22 is slidable in a respective radial guide 24 of the frame. The radial guide 24 constrains the jaw carriage 22 to travel along a radial path toward and away from the central axis of the closed frame.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a jaw pad 26 that is mounted on the jaw carriage 22 for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface toward the central axis of the closed frame. Because the jaw pad 26 pivots relative to the jaw carriage 22, the jaw pad 26 bears on the pipe 20 without requiring a tool specific pipe diameter.

A carriage spring 42 biases each jaw carriage 22 outward, away from the central axis of the closed frame. When the releasable latch 18 is released, the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22 outward and lift the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened.

The segmented cam ring

A cam ring 30 is retained in an annular guide 36 of the frame, as shown in FIG. 2. The annular guide 36 retains the cam ring 30 while allowing the cam ring 30 to rotate through a limited stroke about the central axis of the closed frame.

The mounting boss 66 stands on the frame outside the annular guide 36, clear of the cam ring 30 and of the jaw carriages 22.

The cam ring 30 is segmented. Referring to FIG. 3, the cam ring 30 comprises a first cam-ring segment 32 and a second cam-ring segment 34. The first cam-ring segment 32 is carried by the first frame half 12 and the second cam-ring segment 34 is carried by the second frame half 14, each segment being retained by the frame half that carries it. Each segment accordingly stays with its own frame half when the frame is opened, and the frame halves can be swung apart without dismantling the drive.

The first cam-ring segment 32 has a hinge-end drive face 44 and a latch-end drive face 48. The second cam-ring segment 34 has a hinge-end drive face 46 and a latch-end drive face 50. The hinge-end drive face 44 and the hinge-end drive face 46 are complementary to one another, and the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 are complementary to one another. Closing the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 at the hinge end and brings the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50 at the latch end, and thereby couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 so that they rotate together as one cam ring 30 about the central axis of the closed frame.

In the closed frame each pair of complementary drive faces transmits circumferential drive from one cam-ring segment to the other, and the complementary drive faces separate when the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are swung apart about the hinge 16.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a follower 40 that is received in a respective oblique slot 38 of the cam ring 30, as shown in FIG. 2. Each oblique slot 38 is inclined to the circumferential direction of the cam ring 30, so that rotation of the cam ring 30 through the limited stroke displaces the follower 40, and with it the jaw carriage 22, along the radial guide 24. The oblique slots 38 are identical in inclination and are distributed circumferentially to match the jaw carriages 22, so that rotation of the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke produces the same inward travel at every jaw carriage 22. The inward travel of the three jaw carriages 22 is thereby synchronized.

The latch drive

The releasable latch 18 carries a wedge 52, as shown in FIG. 4. Moving the releasable latch 18 drives the wedge 52 against a ring drive face 54 of the cam ring 30, shown in FIG. 3, and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke.

The releasable latch 18 has a first position and a second position. In the first position the releasable latch 18 holds the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 around the pipe 20 without clamping the pipe 20. The second position is an over-center position, in which the releasable latch 18 has driven the wedge 52 and the cam ring 30 and clamps the pipe 20.

Referring again to FIG. 4, the releasable latch 18 comprises a latch handle 56, a latch housing 58 and a force-limiting spring stack 62. The force-limiting spring stack 62 lies in a drive path between the latch handle 56 and the wedge 52.

Once all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, further movement of the latch handle 56 toward the over-center position compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than forcing one jaw pad 26 farther than the others. The latch travel that remains after contact is therefore taken up by the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the clamping load is set by the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than by the position at which the releasable latch 18 comes to rest.

An indicator pin 64 is visible on the releasable latch 18 and moves relative to a fixed edge 60 of the latch housing 58 when the force-limiting spring stack 62 enters a predetermined compression range. The position of the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60 is a mechanical report that the split pipe clamp 10 is loaded within that range. The indicator pin 64 reports clamp loading and does not measure the diameter of the pipe 20.

Installation and removal

To install the split pipe clamp 10, an operator opens the releasable latch 18 and swings the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 20 and closes them, which brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 and the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50, and so couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 into a single cam ring 30. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the first position, in which the frame halves are held around the pipe 20 without clamping. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the over-center position. The wedge 52 bears on the ring drive face 54 and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke, the oblique slots 38 advance all of the jaw carriages 22 inward together, and the jaw pads 26 pivot and seat on the pipe 20. Latch travel remaining after the jaw pads 26 seat compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the operator observes the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60.

To remove the split pipe clamp 10, the operator releases the releasable latch 18. The force-limiting spring stack 62 unloads and the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22, lifting the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are then swung apart about the hinge 16, and the hinge-end drive face 44, the hinge-end drive face 46, the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 separate so that the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 travel with their own frame halves. The split pipe clamp 10 is reusable.

The essential relationship of the arrangement described here is that closure of the frame halves couples the cam-ring segments, that travel of the releasable latch 18 drives the coupled cam ring 30, that the oblique slots 38 synchronize the radial travel of the jaw carriages 22, and that the force-limiting spring stack 62 accommodates the remaining latch travel. The features described above may be combined in ways other than those expressly set out, and modifications within the understanding of a person skilled in the art fall within the scope of the claims that follow.

The frame carries a mounting boss 66. The mounting boss 66 supports a sensor, a tool or a conduit on the split pipe clamp 10. The mounting boss 66 does not participate in advancing or synchronizing the jaw carriages 22.

Jaw carriages and jaw pads

Referring to FIG. 2, each jaw carriage 22 is slidable in a respective radial guide 24 of the frame. The radial guide 24 constrains the jaw carriage 22 to travel along a radial path toward and away from the central axis of the closed frame.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a jaw pad 26 that is mounted on the jaw carriage 22 for pivoting movement and that presents a concave bearing surface toward the central axis of the closed frame. Because the jaw pad 26 pivots relative to the jaw carriage 22, the jaw pad 26 bears on the pipe 20 without requiring a tool specific pipe diameter.

A carriage spring 42 biases each jaw carriage 22 outward, away from the central axis of the closed frame. When the releasable latch 18 is released, the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22 outward and lift the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened.

The segmented cam ring

A cam ring 30 is retained in an annular guide 36 of the frame, as shown in FIG. 2. The annular guide 36 retains the cam ring 30 while allowing the cam ring 30 to rotate through a limited stroke about the central axis of the closed frame.

The mounting boss 66 stands on the frame outside the annular guide 36.

The cam ring 30 is segmented. Referring to FIG. 3, the cam ring 30 comprises a first cam-ring segment 32 and a second cam-ring segment 34. The first cam-ring segment 32 is carried by the first frame half 12 and the second cam-ring segment 34 is carried by the second frame half 14, each segment being retained by the frame half that carries it. Each segment accordingly stays with its own frame half when the frame is opened, and the frame halves can be swung apart without dismantling the drive.

The first cam-ring segment 32 has a hinge-end drive face 44 and a latch-end drive face 48. The second cam-ring segment 34 has a hinge-end drive face 46 and a latch-end drive face 50. The hinge-end drive face 44 and the hinge-end drive face 46 are complementary to one another, and the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 are complementary to one another. Closing the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 at the hinge end and brings the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50 at the latch end, and thereby couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 so that they rotate together as one cam ring 30 about the central axis of the closed frame.

In the closed frame each pair of complementary drive faces transmits circumferential drive from one cam-ring segment to the other, and the complementary drive faces separate when the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are swung apart about the hinge 16.

Each jaw carriage 22 carries a follower 40 that is received in a respective oblique slot 38 of the cam ring 30, as shown in FIG. 2. Each oblique slot 38 is inclined to the circumferential direction of the cam ring 30, so that rotation of the cam ring 30 through the limited stroke displaces the follower 40, and with it the jaw carriage 22, along the radial guide 24. The oblique slots 38 are arranged so that rotation of the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke produces the same inward travel at every jaw carriage 22. The inward travel of the three jaw carriages 22 is thereby synchronized.

The latch drive

The releasable latch 18 carries a wedge 52, as shown in FIG. 4. Moving the releasable latch 18 drives the wedge 52 against a ring drive face 54 of the cam ring 30, shown in FIG. 3, and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke.

The releasable latch 18 has a first position and a second position. In the first position the releasable latch 18 holds the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 around the pipe 20 without clamping the pipe 20. The second position is an over-center position, in which the releasable latch 18 has driven the wedge 52 and the cam ring 30 and clamps the pipe 20.

Referring again to FIG. 4, the releasable latch 18 comprises a latch handle 56, a latch housing 58 and a force-limiting spring stack 62. The force-limiting spring stack 62 lies in a drive path between the latch handle 56 and the wedge 52.

Once all of the jaw pads 26 have contacted the pipe 20, further movement of the latch handle 56 toward the over-center position compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than forcing one jaw pad 26 farther than the others. The latch travel that remains after contact is therefore taken up by the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the clamping load is set by the force-limiting spring stack 62 rather than by the position at which the releasable latch 18 comes to rest.

An indicator pin 64 is visible on the releasable latch 18 and moves relative to a fixed edge 60 of the latch housing 58 when the force-limiting spring stack 62 enters a predetermined compression range. The position of the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60 is a mechanical report that the split pipe clamp 10 is loaded within that range. The indicator pin 64 reports clamp loading and does not measure the diameter of the pipe 20.

Installation and removal

To install the split pipe clamp 10, an operator opens the releasable latch 18 and swings the first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 apart about the hinge 16. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 20 and closes them, which brings the hinge-end drive face 44 into engagement with the hinge-end drive face 46 and the latch-end drive face 48 into engagement with the latch-end drive face 50, and so couples the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 into a single cam ring 30. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the first position, in which the frame halves are held around the pipe 20 without clamping. The operator then moves the releasable latch 18 to the over-center position. The wedge 52 bears on the ring drive face 54 and rotates the coupled cam ring 30 through the limited stroke, the oblique slots 38 advance all of the jaw carriages 22 inward together, and the jaw pads 26 pivot and seat on the pipe 20. Latch travel remaining after the jaw pads 26 seat compresses the force-limiting spring stack 62, and the operator observes the indicator pin 64 relative to the fixed edge 60.

To remove the split pipe clamp 10, the operator releases the releasable latch 18. The force-limiting spring stack 62 unloads and the carriage springs 42 retract the jaw carriages 22, lifting the jaw pads 26 off the pipe 20 before the frame halves are opened. The first frame half 12 and the second frame half 14 are then swung apart about the hinge 16, and the hinge-end drive face 44, the hinge-end drive face 46, the latch-end drive face 48 and the latch-end drive face 50 separate so that the first cam-ring segment 32 and the second cam-ring segment 34 travel with their own frame halves. The split pipe clamp 10 is reusable.

The essential relationship of the arrangement described here is that closure of the frame halves couples the cam-ring segments, that travel of the releasable latch 18 drives the coupled cam ring 30, that the oblique slots 38 synchronize the radial travel of the jaw carriages 22, and that the force-limiting spring stack 62 accommodates the remaining latch travel. The features described above may be combined in ways other than those expressly set out, and modifications within the understanding of a person skilled in the art fall within the scope of the claims that follow.
